opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's the natural question, because if you took the idea literally — give every document its own dedicated set of neurons — your model would grow linearly with the size of your training corpus, and that's obviously not workable at pretraining scale.

So the way we think about it is that you don't need exclusive neurons per document; you need neurons that are *consistently* associated with a document. In practice, each document, or sequence, gets assigned a subset of these "memorization" neurons, typically through something like a hash of a document ID, so whenever that document shows up during training, the same subset gets activated. Different documents overlap in which neurons they use, so the total number of extra neurons stays fixed and modest, maybe a fraction of the MLP width, rather than scaling with the number of documents.

The intuition for why sharing still works comes from how memorization versus generalization plays out during training. The shared, general-purpose neurons see every example, so they get pushed toward features that are useful across lots of documents. The memorization neurons for a given document only get gradient signal when that document, or the handful of documents it collides with, appears. So they become a natural place to absorb the idiosyncratic, sequence-specific stuff, the things you'd need to regurgitate a particular passage verbatim. Since the collisions are essentially random, the interference between documents sharing a neuron tends to look like noise rather than something coherent that the model can exploit for generalization.

Then at the end, you can drop or zero out those memorization neurons, and ideally you keep most of the general capability while removing a lot of the verbatim memorization.

There's a real tradeoff in how you size things. If the memorization pool is too small, you get too many collisions, the neurons start encoding things that are shared across documents, and memorization leaks back into the general neurons. If it's too large, you're spending parameters that you throw away at inference time. So it's a knob, and part of what we were trying to understand, both empirically and with simpler theoretical models, is that you can get a lot of the isolation benefit with a fairly small budget. You don't need anything like one neuron per document. You just need enough randomness and consistency in the assignment that the training dynamics do the separation for you.

r001.rationale: The response describes documents receiving hashed, overlapping subsets of memorization neurons, but does not state that their activation subspaces are approximately orthogonal.

r002.rationale: The response mentions random collisions but does not state that randomly chosen directions in a high-dimensional space are approximately orthogonal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the question of model size really is the question of capacity, and capacity is what's being traded off against memorization. The way I like to frame it is: a model has some finite budget of parameters, and every time it memorizes a specific document, some of that budget gets spent on something that doesn't generalize. So if you're asking how we think about limiting size, it's really asking how much of that budget are we willing to let go toward memorizing the long tail.

And the interesting thing is that this isn't a clean, mechanistic allocation. It's not like the model goes, "okay, these neurons are for document seventeen." In practice what you see is more of a competition. Documents that are repeated many times in the training data, or that are very distinctive, tend to win more capacity. Rare documents that look like a lot of other things get compressed into shared representations instead. So when you shrink the model, the first casualties are those rare, unique things, which is often exactly what you'd want from a privacy standpoint, but exactly what you don't want if that long tail contains knowledge you actually need.

So I'd push back a little on the idea that limiting size is a good lever on its own. It's a blunt instrument. What we've been finding is that the more useful questions are about how you structure the training process. Things like how many times a document appears, whether you deduplicate, how you schedule the data, and even what you do at fine-tuning time can have a much larger effect on memorization than just cutting parameters. In some of our work we've seen that models can memorize surprisingly well even when they're small, as long as the signal is repeated enough, and conversely, large models don't necessarily memorize more per document if you're careful about the data.

The other piece I'd add is that memorization and generalization aren't always in opposition, which complicates the whole neuron allocation picture. Some memorization is actually load bearing. Knowing specific facts, specific names, specific rare entities is memorization, and you want that. So the goal isn't to minimize memorization globally. It's to get the model to spend capacity on the kind of memorization that's useful and not on, say, verbatim training strings that leak sensitive information. And right now we don't have great tools for steering that allocation directly, which is honestly one of the more open problems in the space.

r001.rationale: The response describes competition for model capacity and shared representations, but does not state that documents can occupy approximately orthogonal activation subspaces within shared neurons.

r002.rationale: It does not mention random directions in a high-dimensional space or their approximate orthogonality.

astra-6.text:
I think of limiting model size as imposing a shared capacity budget. If you imagine allocating a separate set of neurons to memorize each document, that strategy becomes expensive as you add more documents. With a smaller model, there’s more pressure to reuse representations across documents—to capture patterns that explain many examples rather than storing every example separately.

But that’s an intuition, not a guarantee that smaller models won’t memorize. And the allocation isn’t literally one set of neurons per document; information can be distributed across the network. The interesting question is what the model chooses to fit with the capacity it has, and how the data and training procedure influence that choice.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared capacity budget and possible reuse of representations, but does not state that documents can be assigned approximately orthogonal activation subspaces within shared neurons.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention randomly chosen directions or their approximate orthogonality in high-dimensional space.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of model size as a capacity budget. If you imagine allocating a separate set of neurons to memorize every document, then the amount you can store is going to grow with the number of parameters. But that picture misses the fact that documents share structure. You’d hope the model learns something reusable, so it doesn’t need to allocate fresh capacity to every new document.

The interesting question is what happens when you constrain that budget. Does the model learn shared patterns because that’s a more efficient way to fit the data, or does it memorize a subset of the documents and do poorly on the rest? Limiting size alone doesn’t tell you which behavior you’ll get. That also depends on the data and the learning process.

r001.rationale: It discusses allocating capacity across documents and shared patterns, but does not state that documents can occupy approximately orthogonal activation subspaces within shared neurons.
